food.text: Kumis was a fermented drink made from mare's milk. It was central to the diet of Turkic and Mongolic peoples across the Central Asian and Siberian steppes, including the Kyrgyz, Kazakhs and Yakuts.
Central Asian cooks baked in tandyr clay ovens fueled by poplar wood, saxaul shrubs and animal dung. These ovens were used to cook flatbread, samsa pastries and meats.

Nomadic peoples in what are now Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan built their diet mainly around meat and dairy. Elsewhere in Central Asia, millet, wheat, rice and barley were the main grains, used to make flatbread and noodles.

Before mid-October 627, heavy snows on the Mongolian–Manchurian grassland covered the ground to a depth of several feet. The nomads' livestock could not graze, and a massive die-off among the animals followed. According to the New Book of Tang, in 628 Taizong mentioned that there had been a frost in midsummer.

Milking a mare for kumis took real skill. The milker knelt on one knee, with a pail propped on the other knee, one arm behind the mare's rear leg and the other in front, while a foal started the milk flow and was pulled aside but kept touching the mare's side.
Mare's milk holds more sugar than cow's or goat's milk. Once fermented into kumis, this gave the drink a higher, though still mild, alcohol content than kefir, typically between 0.7 and 2.5 percent.
Turkic culinary traditions shaped much of Central Asian cooking. They contributed dishes such as manti dumplings, a wheat porridge called sumalak, and an assortment of dairy products.
Besh barmak, a lamb dish eaten by hand, was a staple in parts of Central Asia. Along with horse meat, it was found mainly in what are now Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, unlike other regions.

In Mongolia, the horse milking season traditionally ran from mid-June to early October. A single mare could yield roughly 1,000 to 1,200 litres of milk in that time, about half of which was left for her foal.
Central Asian nomads reportedly used freeze distillation to strengthen kumis. The fermented mare's milk could also be further distilled into a stronger drink called arkhi.

Kumis was drunk and enjoyed much like beer, yet it is technically closer to wine. Its alcohol comes directly from fermenting milk sugars, unlike grain-based beer, whose starches must first be converted into sugar.

art.text: The Buddhist art of Bamiyan culminated in the 6th century AD with two monumental statues of Gautama Buddha carved into a cliff. They stand in the Bamyan valley of central Afghanistan, 130 kilometres northwest of Kabul, at an elevation of 2,500 metres.

Islamic art spread across Central Asia with the rule of the Umayyad and Abbasid Arabs. Buildings following Islamic standards went up throughout the land, such as the Abbasid mosque of Afrasiab in Samarkand, built around 750 to 825 CE.

In the 10th century, as the Samanid dynasty ruled Khurasan and Transoxiana, distinctive regional features began to appear in Central Asian Islamic architecture. Baked brick became the dominant medium for both construction and decoration, and ceramic tile was used to decorate surfaces.

Carbon dating of the structural components of the Buddhas of Bamiyan gave two different dates. The smaller 38 m Eastern Buddha was built around 570 AD, and the larger 55 m Western Buddha around 618 AD.

From the 4th to the 6th centuries AD, China's Northern dynasties, ruled by the nomadic Xianbei, traded with Central Asia, often through Sogdian traders. Northern Wei art absorbed Indian and Central Asian traditions along these routes, including Buddhism, which flourished under the Northern dynasties.

Palaces and residences around Merv, in present-day Turkmenistan, have been studied as examples of secular architecture from this period. They shared many features with earlier Sasanian and Sogdian architecture. Recurring elements included iwans and domed chambers.

Numerous Central Asian works of art have been found in the tombs of the Northern Wei, the Northern Qi and the Northern Zhou. They are especially decorated silverware and jewelry, evidence of how far such objects travelled along the trade routes.

Muqarnas, a form of three-dimensional geometric vaulting, seems to have developed in Iran and Central Asia around the 10th century. It began as a transitional architectural element, initially a tripartite subdivision of the more traditional squinch, and later became characteristic of Islamic architecture more widely.

Merv-area residences up to the 8th century seem to have had halls with wooden pillars and roofs. Those that probably date to the 9th century seem to have favored domes and vaulted ceilings. They also had stucco decoration executed in the styles of Samarra.
For mosques in Central Asia around the 10th century, the hypostyle layout of early Islamic architecture continued to be used. It now stood alongside new types, such as multi-domed mosques.

The Sasanian tradition of building caravanserais along trade routes continued after the Sasanian era. The remains of one such structure in southern Turkmenistan show a central courtyard surrounded by arcaded galleries with domed roofs.

war.text: At the Battle of Talas in 751, an Arab army decisively defeated a Tang force. The defeat expelled Chinese influence from western Central Asia.

In 630, Tang armies captured areas of the Ordos Desert, modern-day Inner Mongolia, and southern Mongolia from the Turks. The Tang began this offensive once their civil war in China had almost ended and the Ordos warlord Liang Shidu had been defeated in 628. In 631 Emperor Taizong sent envoys with gold and silk to the Eastern Turkic tribes to buy the release of enslaved Chinese prisoners captured during the fall of the Sui, and 80,000 Chinese men and women were freed.

Steppe nomads and the settled peoples in and around Central Asia were long marked by conflict. The nomadic lifestyle was well suited to warfare, and the steppe horse riders became some of the most militarily potent people in the world, limited only by their lack of internal unity. Periodically great leaders or changing conditions organised several tribes into one almost unstoppable force, as in the Hun invasion of Europe, the Five Barbarians rebellions in China and, most notably, the Mongol conquest of much of Eurasia. The main Turkic migration across Central Asia took place between the 6th and 11th centuries.

The Uyghur Khaganate built a fortified capital, Ordu-Baliq, as a commercial center along the Silk Road. It had concentric walls, lookout towers, stables, and a palace protected by two gates and moats filled with water.

Civil war in China was almost totally diminished by 626, and in 628 the Ordos Chinese warlord Liang Shidu was defeated. After these internal conflicts, the Tang turned outward and began an offensive against the Turks.

After the Arab victory at Talas in 751, Middle Eastern influences dominated western Central Asia for the next several centuries. Large-scale Islamization did not begin until the 9th century, alongside the fragmentation of Abbasid political authority and the rise of local dynasties like the Samanids.

The Islamic expansion reached Central Asia in the 8th century AD but had no significant demographic impact. The region's population changes came instead from the Turkic migrations of the 6th to 11th centuries.

literature.text: Khotanese literary works were written in a dialect of the Saka language used by the Saka Kingdom of Khotan, on the southern branch of the Silk Road. They centered mostly on Buddhist texts and were produced mainly between the 5th and 10th centuries.

The Orkhon inscriptions are bilingual memorial steles in Middle Chinese and Old Turkic, erected by the Göktürks in the early 8th century in Mongolia's Orkhon Valley. They honor the Turkic princes Kul Tigin and his brother Bilge Qaghan, and recount the legendary origins of the Turks, their subjugation by the Tang dynasty, and their liberation by Ilterish Qaghan. Bilge Qaghan says the sons of the nobles became the bondsmen of the Chinese and their unsullied daughters became slaves. The fragmentary text also seems to describe conquests against the Kyrgyz and the Tangut and the death of Kul Tigin in battle.

The Old Turkic script, also called the Göktürk or Orkhon script, was used by the Göktürks and other Turkic khanates from the 8th to 10th centuries to record the Old Turkic language. It is thought to have been derived from or inspired by the Sogdian script, and words were usually written from right to left.

Inscriptions in the Old Turkic script have been found across a vast area, from Mongolia and Xinjiang in the east to the Balkans in the west, with a Yenisei variant known from 9th-century Yenisei Kyrgyz inscriptions. Dated between the 8th and 10th centuries, these texts are mostly epitaphs, though graffiti and short inscriptions on objects like bronze mirrors also survive.
The Old Turkic script was invented in the first half of the sixth century. This was during the rise of the First Turkic Khaganate, founded by the Ashina clan of the Göktürks.

The Oghuz Turks were the branch of the Turkic peoples that migrated towards western Asia and eastern Europe through Transoxiana, beginning in the 9th century CE. Their oral traditions later gave rise to the Book of Dede Korkut.

Irk Bitig, or the Book of Omens, is a 9th-century manuscript on divination discovered in the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang by Aurel Stein in 1907. It is the only known complete manuscript written in the Old Turkic script and is an important source for early Turkic mythology.

The Old Uyghur script developed from writing traditions ultimately derived from the Aramaic script through the intermediary of the Sogdian script, and was used for Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian texts in Turpan. Sogdian communities active along the Eurasian trade routes played an important role in transmitting literacy to Turkic populations.

Tonyukuk was the supreme commander and adviser to four successive Göktürk khagans, including Ilterish Qaghan and Bilge Qaghan. Around 716, his biography, achievements and advice on state administration were carved in the Old Turkic script on two steles erected near present-day Ulaanbaatar's Nalaikh district.

Bilge Qaghan, born Ashina Mojilian, was the fourth qaghan of the Second Turkic Khaganate, living from 683 to 734. He was poisoned by Buyruk Chor, but did not die at once and had time to put Buyruk Chor's family to death before he died on 25 November 734. After his death from poisoning, several steles were erected near the Orkhon River, and the Orkhon inscriptions on them, which describe his accomplishments, are the first known texts in Old Turkic.

Manichaeism was the official religion of the Uyghur Khaganate until the Khaganate collapsed in 840. After that, the Tang court closed nearly all Manichaean temples in China and later turned to killing. In 843 Emperor Wuzong of Tang ordered all Manichaean clerics killed, and over half died. The authorities made them look like Buddhists first, shaving their heads and dressing them as Buddhist monks, and then killed them. Its canon of scripture included seven works attributed to the prophet Mani, six of them originally written in Syriac.
The First Turkic Khaganate invented its own Old Turkic script. Yet its earliest official texts and even its coins were written in Sogdian rather than Turkic.

In the early eighth century, the Göktürks carved the Orkhon inscriptions into two stone steles in the Orkhon Valley, now in Mongolia. Written partly in the Old Turkic alphabet alongside Middle Chinese, the inscriptions recorded the legendary origins of the Turks and the golden age of their history. They also recorded the Turks' subjugation by the Tang dynasty, and the text says the Turkic nobles' sons became bondsmen and their daughters slaves of the Chinese, until Ilterish Qaghan liberated them.

The Irk Bitig, a 9th-century Old Turkic divination manuscript, refers to the sky god Tengri as 'Türük Tängrisi', meaning 'God of Turks'. Tengrism, the prevailing belief system of the Göktürks, can be identified through such written texts as well as the Orkhon inscriptions.

Kul Tigin, a general and prince of the Second Turkic Khaganate, died suddenly on 27 February 731. A stele inscribed in both Turkic and Chinese was erected in his memory at Khoshoo Tsaidam, the same site as the Orkhon inscription honoring his brother Bilge Qaghan.

Old Uyghur was first written in the 5th century using the Sogdian alphabet, and while that alphabet was still in use it was also recorded in the Old Turkic script from the 6th to 9th centuries. Only in the 10th century did this writing evolve into the distinct Old Uyghur alphabet.

According to its colophon, Irk Bitig was written on the fifteenth day of the second month of a year of the tiger at the Taygüntan Manichaean monastery. It was copied there by an anonymous monk for his 'elder brother', General İtaçuk, sometime during the 9th or 10th century.

science.text: In July 751, Tang and Abbasid armies clashed at the Talas River over control of the regions surrounding the Syr Darya. Arabic sources put Chinese losses at 45,000 to 50,000 dead, with 20,000 to 25,000 more taken captive, while the Tongdian counts 30,000 deaths and the Old Book of Tang 20,000. Chinese prisoners captured in the battle are said to have introduced papermaking to the peoples of West Asia, though the article calls this account unlikely to be factual.

Samarkand's paper industry began around the 8th century, about the same time as the paper mills of Baghdad. Its handmade mulberry paper replaced papyrus and became preferred over parchment for Qurans and miniatures, because it was lighter and easier to store.

Al-Farghani, an astronomer whose name suggests he came from Farghana in modern Uzbekistan, became one of the most famous astronomers of the 9th century. His best-known book, Elements of astronomy on the celestial motions, summarized Ptolemy's Almagest with revised and more accurate experimental data.

Al-Biruni was born in Kath in Khwarazm and spent his first twenty-five years there. He studied mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy, among other subjects, and dabbled in most of the other sciences of his day, growing into a leading polymath.
Paper reached Samarkand along the Silk Road. Sogdian paper letters to Samarkandi merchants have been dated to 313 CE, and Chinese xuan paper was a trade good there by the early 8th century.
Al-Farghani joined a team of scientists under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun in Baghdad that calculated the diameter of the Earth. They did this by measuring the length of a meridian arc.

Al-Farabi's birthplace could have been any of several places in Central Asia, such as Farab (Otrar) on the Syr Darya in modern Kazakhstan. Although he was not intrinsically a scientist, his works incorporate astronomy, mathematics, cosmology and physics.

Samarkand made two kinds of paper. Rag paper was preferred for religious texts, and mulberry paper was used for general purposes. A defining step was burnishing, in which a rock or shell was rubbed over the sheet to smooth its surface.

A popular story credits Chinese papermakers captured by the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas in 751 with bringing paper to Samarkand. The origin is likely apocryphal, because archaeologists have found paper in the region that predates the battle.

Al-Farabi noted that music borrows principles from mathematics. He argued that musical performance and the art of hearing were ideal judges of whether certain theoretical propositions were valid, even if the music sometimes contradicted more concrete mathematical calculations.
Al-Farghani's astronomy books spread widely in Arabic and Latin. Centuries later, Christopher Columbus used his calculations for voyages to America, but mistakenly read Arabic miles as Roman miles.

politics.text: In the 6th and 7th centuries, the Hephthalites were the most powerful of the nomad groups in Central Asia. They controlled much of the region. Their rise came once foreign powers had been expelled, and several indigenous empires formed.

The Tang dynasty of China expanded westwards and controlled large parts of Central Asia. It held them both directly and indirectly, through its Turkic vassals. Tang China also actively supported the Turkification of Central Asia while extending its cultural influence.

The main migration of Turkic peoples took place between the 6th and 11th centuries. During this time they spread across most of Central Asia. The movement slowly changed the Eurasian Steppe from a region of Indo-European and Iranian-speaking groups to a more heterogeneous one.

The House of Seljuk was a branch of the Kınık Oğuz Turks. In the 10th century they lived on the edge of the Muslim world, north of the Caspian and Aral Seas, in the Yabghu Khaganate of the Oğuz confederacy. This was the homeland the Seljuks later left for Anatolia.

A volcanic eruption in 626 caused the weather to cool precipitously in Mongolia and northern China, and in the spring or autumn of 627 severe snow caused a mass die-off among the Turkic nomads' livestock. Rather than helping the struggling population, ruler Illig Qaghan demanded greater contributions from subject tribes, and they openly revolted by the summer of 628. When his nephew Ashina Shibobi failed to put down the uprisings, Illig had him flogged, then attacked him, and the revolts helped bring down the Eastern Turkic Khaganate.
politics.source_title: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks

politics.text: The Tang Chinese were defeated by the Abbasid Caliphate at the Battle of Talas in 751. The defeat ended the Tang dynasty's western expansion. It also marked the end of 150 years of Chinese influence in Central Asia.
In the 8th century, the Islamic expansion reached Central Asia. It had no significant demographic impact on the region. The Abbasid Caliphate's victory at Talas came in the same century.
After the Tang defeat at Talas, the Tibetan Empire took the chance to rule portions of Central Asia and South Asia. The Tang withdrawal left a gap that another power moved to fill.

philosophy.text: The Religious Annals of Khotan describes two paths into the Dharma. Śrāvakas enter through the Four Noble Truths, while Mahayana bodhisattvas enter through non-conceptualization and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Though it covers both the Śrāvakayāna and the Mahāyāna, the text gives the Mahāyāna preeminence.

Khotan was independent but intermittently under Chinese control during the Han and Tang dynasties. Its indigenous royal dynasty used only names of Indian origin, showing how deeply Indian religion and culture had taken root there.

In the 7th century CE, Yijing grouped the Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka and Kāśyapīya together as sub-sects of the Sarvāstivāda. He stated that these three were not prevalent in the "five parts of India" but were found in parts of Oḍḍiyāna, Khotan and Kucha.

Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī, an Eastern Iranic scholar in service to the Ghaznavids, reported that around the start of the 10th century the monasteries in Bactria were still functioning. They included Nava Vihāra, and were decorated with Buddha frescoes.

culture.text: Buddhism dominated Central Asia before the arrival of Islam, mostly in Mahayana forms. It was especially prevalent along the Silk Road, and its history there is closely tied to the transmission of Buddhism along that route during the first millennium CE.
Buddhism and Zoroastrianism were the major faiths in Central Asia before Islam arrived. Among the Turkic peoples, Tengrism was the leading religion.

The main migration of Turkic peoples took place between the 6th and 11th centuries, when they spread across most of Central Asia. Turkic languages largely replaced the Iranian languages once spoken by Bactrians, Sogdians and Chorasmians. The Islamic expansion of the 8th century had no significant demographic impact.

The Uyghurs adopted the writing system of the Sogdians, along with religious faiths such as Manichaeism, Buddhism, and Christianity. They looked to the Sogdians as mentors while gradually taking over their role as Silk Road traders.

Khotan was an independent, fervently Buddhist city-state whose indigenous dynasty had royal names that were all Indian in origin. By the late 9th or early 10th century it boasted some 400 temples, four times the number recorded by Xuanzang around 630 CE.

In Balkh stood the Buddhist monastery of Nava Vihara, meaning "New Monastery", which served as the center of Central Asian Buddhist learning for centuries. Soon after the Sassanian Persian dynasty fell to the Muslims in 651, Balkh came under Muslim rule in 663 and the monastery was conquered, though it kept functioning for at least another century. In 715, after the Abbasid Caliphate crushed an insurrection in Balkh, many Persian Buddhist monks fled east along the Silk Road to Khotan and onward into China.

A Tibetan manuscript called The Religious Annals of Khotan, found at Dunhuang, may date to the 8th century CE. It describes the first appearance of Buddhism in Khotan, including the eight major tutelary deities of the city, and gives preeminence to the Mahayana.
The name "Mongol" first appeared in the mid-10th century Chinese Old Book of Tang. It described a tribe of the Shiwei who resided in the Argun River basin in the 9th century.
Within Ordu-Baliq, specific areas were set aside for trade and handcrafts. At the center of the city stood palaces and temples, including a monastery.

Around the start of the 10th century, the scholar Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī reported that monasteries in Bactria, including Nava Vihara, were still functioning. He said they were decorated with Buddha frescoes.
